[MUQATIL:50:11/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Rain revives barren land without vegetation, which then grows; this whole provision is for God's servants.
[MUQATIL:50:11/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | People will likewise emerge from their graves through water, as plants emerge from earth through water.
[MUQATIL:50:11/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The signs of rain and growth make people recognize God's oneness and power to resurrect.
[MAJAZ:v2p223/r1] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | Al-khurūj refers to the Day of Resurrection; al-ʿAjjāj’s verse calls it the day of rising.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p43/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Rizqan has two accusative analyses: a cognate object (“provided them provision”) or a purpose object (“grew these things for sustenance”).
[ZAJJAJ:v5p43/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Just as God created these things, He will raise people from the dead.
[NAHHAS:v4p221/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq parses rizqan as either a verbal noun or an object of purpose.
[NAHHAS:v4p221/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The revived town is barren, without crops or vegetation.
[NAHHAS:v4p221/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Kadhālika al-khurūj is a subject-predicate clause; al-khurūj means coming forth from graves, as God raises people with water as plants grow.
[NAHHAS:v4p221/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq says God will resurrect you just as He created these things.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p343/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Provision is blessed rain and what it produces: plants, harvested grain, and clustered palm fruit.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p343/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The dead town proves resurrection: re-creating what had a source is easier than first creation, and reviving dead plants shows God can restore people for recompense.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p226/r7] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Just as God sends water to revive dry land, He can gather people for resurrection; raising the dead is no more difficult than reviving the land.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v20p387/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abu Ishaq parses rizqan either as an implied cognate object, “We provided them provision,” or as a purpose object, “We brought forth these things for provision.”
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v20p387/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The emergence from graves is like the creation of plants; God likewise brings the dead out, as in 7:57. | mentions 7:57
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v20p387/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says rain falls like men's seminal fluid and flesh and bones grow upon the dead.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v20p387/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil compares people emerging from their graves through rain to plants emerging from earth through rain.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:50:5-11/r7] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | God provides these things as sustenance for His servants.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:50:5-11/r8] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | God revives a dead land with rain just as people will emerge from their graves.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p357#2/r10] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | “By it” refers to the rain; God grows vegetation in a dead town.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p357#2/r11] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Just as rain revives the dead land, people will come forth from their graves.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p357#2/r9] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The phrase means that God made these things sustenance for the servants, with the verb understood.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p385#2/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Rizqan may mean We grew them as provision, since growing entails provision, or be a purpose clause: We grew them to provide for people.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p385#2/r7] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Just as God revives this dead land, He will bring people to life after death.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p385#2/r8] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The kāf in thus is nominative as the subject of an equative clause.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p157#3/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The town is described as dead with an ellipsis understood as rain or land.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p157#3/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Most readers lighten mayyitan; Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid read it with gemination.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p157#3/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The signs just mentioned exemplify and prove resurrection; al-khurūj means emerging from the graves.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p157#3/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Rizqan is an accusative verbal noun, and the pronoun in bihi refers to the rain.
[TABRISI:50:11/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God made the plants and other growths provisions for His servants; all provision is from God, by His direct act or by causing it, though people may idiomatically be said to provide for others.
[TABRISI:50:11/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The water sent from heaven revives a barren, drought-stricken land that had grown nothing.
[TABRISI:50:11/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | As God brings dead land to life with water, He will bring the dead out of their graves; power over either act entails power over the other.
[TABRISI:50:11/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | People doubt resurrection because they regularly see rain revive land but have no customary experience of dead humans returning; reflection shows both acts are within God's power.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p8#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The plants and fruits are produced as provision for people.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p8#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The land is revived by rain.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p8#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | In the same way, people will emerge from their graves.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p136#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Rizqan is accusative either as a cognate accusative, since growing the plants is provision, or as a purpose accusative, since they are grown to provide for people.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p136#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One explanation is that the heavens and earth point to creation and resurrection, while fruits as provision point to continued sustenance after resurrection; the passage separates these proofs by beginning the water-and-growth discussion afterward. | mentions 50:8, 50:9
[RAZI-FULL:v28p136#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second explanation names the obvious benefit of fruit as provision, while the sky's role in providing sustenance is less obvious to people, though it is the source of provision by God's decree and has other benefits.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p136#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A third explanation says “provision” stresses God's beneficence, making the deniers' rejection especially reprehensible as denial of their benefactor.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p136#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The earlier proof is for every penitent servant, but provision reaches all; the penitent eats gratefully and remembers God, while others eat like livestock. | mentions 50:8
[RAZI-FULL:v28p136#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “We revived with it a dead land” is coordinated with “We grew by it” in the preceding verse. | mentions 50:9
[RAZI-FULL:v28p136#3/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | If crop growth shows sustenance after resurrection, reviving dead land also proves resurrection; it follows the provision evidence because the heavens and earth already established resurrection, before the passage returns to this proof.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p136#3/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Alternatively, reviving land means water greens it and produces flowers, a more widespread adornment than crops; although greenery comes first, crops and fruit are mentioned first as the greater blessing.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p137/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The feminine marker may be present or omitted with mayyit because it is a lightened form of mayyit, and faʿīl as an active adjective can take feminine marking.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p137/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Faʿīl does not mark gender here because distinguishing agent from patient matters more than distinguishing masculine from feminine patients; faʿīl serves both active and passive senses without a distinguishing letter, unlike mafʿūl.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p137/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī explains the feminine suffix in “the dead earth” at 36:33 because earth is described as an agent, whereas “dead town” omits it because the town's underlying state is life; he compares “a good town” at 34:15, where the active sense is clear and the suffix appears. | mentions 36:33, 34:15
[RAZI-FULL:v28p138/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The dead emerge at resurrection as plants emerge when rain revives a dead land: the earth splits and they come out.
[RAZI-FULL:v28p138/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The wording supports reading الرجْع in 50:3 as return (intransitive): if they denied extraction, the fitting answer would have said إخراج, but it says خروج. | mentions 50:3
[RAZI-FULL:v28p138/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, extraction and خروج are cause and effect: denying the cause entails denying the effect, so God emphatically affirms the effect after they denied both. | mentions 50:3
[QURTUBI-FULL:50:10-11/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Rizqan can be an object with an implied “We provided,” a complement of the planting understood as provision, or a purpose expression; provision is what is made ready for use.
[QURTUBI-FULL:50:10-11/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | As God revives dead land by rain, He will bring people alive from their graves; the resurrection is likened to the land's revival.
[QURTUBI-FULL:50:10-11/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The kāf in kathālika is in the predicate position of an initial clause; maytan is masculine because the intende

d referent is the place, though maytatan would also be valid.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:50:11-13/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | رزقا is either the purpose of growing plants or a verbal noun, since growth itself is provision.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:50:11-13/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The land revived by water is barren and has no growth.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:50:11-13/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | As the land comes alive, people emerge alive after death.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p171#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Rizqan means We grew the crops as provision, either a verbal noun not formed from the verb anbatnā or a purpose object meaning We grew them to feed people.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p171#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | By that water God revived a town whose vegetation had dried up.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p171#2/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | People will likewise emerge alive after death: reviving dead land resembles reviving the dead.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p171#2/r4] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The kāf is nominative as the subject.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p531#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Most readers lighten ميتا, while Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid double the yāʾ; the resurrection of people is likened to reviving a dead land.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v9p531#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The vegetation examples distinguish yearly picked produce whose plant remains, crops sown for one or two years, and mixed kinds; crops are mostly food while fruits are largely treats and sometimes food.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:11/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | رزقا may be a circumstantial accusative meaning “provided for” or “possessing provision.”
[SAMIN-DURR:50:11/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | It may be a verbal noun related to أنبتنا, since this growth is itself provision.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:11/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | It may instead be a purpose accusative.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:11/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | للعباد may be an adjective, attach to the verbal noun, or be its object with an extra lām.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:11/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | به refers to water; ميتا describes بلدة and is masculine because the noun is treated as a place.
[SAMIN-DURR:50:11/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · العامة | reports | The common reading lightens; Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid read with doubling.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p396#2/r10] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The witnessed revival of dead land exemplifies resurrection: God likewise revives the dead, and this visible sign of power is more evident than what resurrection-deniers reject. | mentions 40:57, 46:33, 41:39
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p396#2/r11] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | He supports the resurrection argument by citing that creating the heavens and earth is greater than creating people, that God can revive the dead, and that revived earth is a sign of that power. | mentions 40:57, 46:33, 41:39
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p396#2/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The produce is provision for all creatures.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p396#2/r9] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Rain revives formerly barren land: it swells, stirs, and grows beautiful plants and flowers, becoming green after having no vegetation.
[BURHAN:v3p333/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن الزبير | reports | Ibn al-Zubayr treats Qaf's move from denial of resurrection to visible signs in the sky and revived land as a comparable shift; these undeniable signs lead to the conclusion that resurrection will likewise occur. | mentions 50:1, 50:6, 50:9
[BURHAN:v3p333/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | After leaving the disbelievers' challenge unanswered and describing the heavens and rain as observable facts they could not deny, God concludes: “Thus is the emergence.” | mentions 50:6, 50:9
[BURHAN:v3p358/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The masculine adjective ميتا is licensed because بلدة is construed as مکان, ‘place’; otherwise it would be feminine.
[NASHR:v2p223/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو جعفر | reports | Abū Jaʿfar doubles the yāʾ in all the listed forms of «الميتة/ميتا», «بلد ميت», and «الحي من الميت والميت من الحي».
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p250/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After the sign of heaven, the argument turns to earth; heaven is more wondrous and majestic, while familiarity with earth and its fruits makes people overlook its evidence. | mentions 50:6
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p250/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Because human nature can pull down what reason elevates, a person returning to God may fear rejection; the passage encourages return by describing provision and revival.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p250/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God provides the fruits as sustenance for His servants.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p250/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Rain revives a dead town, just as the dead will emerge from their graves.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p251/r16] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God caused these plants to grow because they form part of the provision He assigned to His servants.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p251/r17] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The feminine ending in town signals its extreme weakness and need for support and stability.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p251/r18] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Calling the town dead further stresses how fully dependent it is on revival.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p251/r19] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Plants emerging from pulverized earth resemble the dead rising from graves, restored as they were in worldly life.
[ITQAN:v3p107/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | A feminine is grammatically masculine when construed by a masculine equivalent: admonition, place, sun or rising body, or the meaning of raḥma; al-Jawharī explains قريب by construing it with iḥsān.
[BURSEVI:v9p86#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The planting is explained as sustenance for God's servants; placing this after the previous verse's signs for reflection teaches that contemplation should take priority over enjoyment of food.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Persian couplet teaches that eating is for living and remembering God, rather than living merely for eating.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الكاشفي | reports | Al-Kāshifī says that reflection on a buried seed's revival and emergence after concealment can lead one to infer the revival of the dead.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The earlier verse chiefly demonstrates divine power through the greatest bodies, mentioning growth secondarily, so it suits 'reflection and reminder'; this verse explains their benefits as sustenance, which follows creation.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Maytan is masculine to agree with the implicit masculine noun balad or makān.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | God revives barren land by making it swell and grow plants and flowers, so it moves after having been still and lifeless.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أبو هريرة | reports | Abū Hurayra reports that when rain came and gutters flowed, the Prophet would say, 'No famine upon you this year.' No grading is given.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The predicate is advanced to restrict the comparison: resurrection from graves is like the wondrous life rain brings to land, with nothing in that resurrection unlike it.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | A report says God sends rain for forty nights, which enters the earth like male seed; flesh, veins, and bones grow, then God revives people and brings them out.
[BURSEVI:v9p87/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Calling the emergence of plants 'revival' and resurrection 'emergence' magnifies vegetation's renewal, makes resurrection seem less difficult, and clarifies their correspondence for people.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | رزقا is purposive: God grows plants to provide for His servants; it modifies فأنبتنا.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Calling plant emergence revival and human resurrection خروج magnifies plant growth, makes resurrection seem easy, and clarifies the analogy.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari takes كذلك as the predicate; al-Alusi says this is the apparent parse, while treating كاف as subject is possible.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Making ذلك الخروج a subject-predicate construction with كاف meaning مثل is possible by analogy with أبو يوسف أبو حنيفة, but al-Alusi calls it contrived.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | By placing provision after insight and reminder, the verse signals that reflection should precede and matter more than bodily enjoyment.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alternatively, رزقا is a cognate verbal noun for أنبتنا, since growing plants is provision, like قعدت جلوسا, or it is a circumstantial “provided for.”
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | به refers to the water.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | A dead town is barren land without growth, made productive so that it swells and sprouts.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The masculine adjective agrees with بلدة as understood in the sense of البلد or place.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو جعفر، خالد | reports | Abu Ja'far and Khalid read ميتا with a strengthened consonant.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Fronting كذلك gives emphatic, restrictive focus; ذلك points to the life just described, and its distance suggests its extraordinary rank.
[ALUSI-FULL:v26p176#5/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Resurrection from the graves is like the striking revival of dead land, not something essentially

[ELMALILI:50:6-15/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The crops and dates are brought forth as provision for God’s servants.
[ELMALILI:50:6-15/r18] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rain restores life to barren, dry ground whose growth had ceased.
[ELMALILI:50:6-15/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Resurrection from graves is like a dead town revived by rain and is no less within God’s power.
[ELMALILI:50:6-15/r20] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · Ebussuud | reports | Abu al-Suʿud says calling plant emergence ihyāʾ and resurrection khurūj magnifies planting, makes resurrection seem easy, and clarifies their likeness.
[ELMALILI:50:6-15/r21] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı also reads an allusion to Islam’s emergence and victory through divine favor, bringing new life from a dead community.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p291/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | After reflection on the heavens and earth, the discourse shifts to recurring cycles of life and death, preparing the proof that resurrection is possible. | mentions 50:6, 50:11
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Drought resembles death because signs of life disappear; vegetation is called life, and cultivating and watering barren land is idiomatically called reviving dead land.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Creation of these beings from nothing proves resurrection possible: restoring already existing, weaker beings is more feasible and easier.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r12] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | prefers | The final clause summarizes the proof of resurrection and is best treated as a resumption or, for those who allow it, a parenthetical close.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r13] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The demonstrative points to reviving dead earth: just so God revives people after death and decay, while magnifying the remarkable resurrection.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r14] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The definite article marks the known emergence of people from graves; al-khuruj became a conventional name for resurrection, as 70:43 and 50:42 show. | mentions 70:43, 50:42
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r15] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Putting the prepositional phrase first draws attention to the predicate's rebuttal of impossibility and makes listeners anticipate the subject.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Provision for the servants is an accusative of purpose, an infinitive meaning so that God may provide and sustain people. | mentions 50:9
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Servants means people as God's servants; the plural of a human slave is instead abid. The phrase is both an argument and a favor.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The provision phrase serves as an argument and a reminder of God's favor.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The verb We gave life is coordinated with the noun provision, which is derived from a verb; the sense is that God provided people and revived land.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The land's revival provides pasture for livestock and wild animals, serving as both proof and favor.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A balda is a tract or section of land.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The lightly pronounced mayyit is synonymous with the doubled form; 36:33 calls dead land a sign for people. | mentions 36:33
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v26p293/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The adjective is masculine with the feminine land because it is understood as balad, a synonym, or as makān, its genus.
[TABATABAI:50:1-4/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | It then recalls God's knowledge and power through creation of the adorned heavens, spread and planted earth, and rain that provides for and revives creation.
[TABATABAI:50:9-14/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Sustenance is that by which life is maintained.
